What is Foraging?
[1] Foraging is identifying, collecting, and eating plants like herbs, fruits, and
nuts that grow wild in nature.
Foraging Guidelines
[2] Here are some rules that every forager should follow:
• [3] Never start solo. It’s essential to begin by partnering up with a local expert
who can teach you the best ways to forage while also keeping you safe.
• [4] Familiarise yourself with the herbs, bushes, and trees around you. Try to
learn as much as possible about the ecosystem of which you are a part.
• [5] Learn to identify the poisonous plants you are likely to encounter. DO
NOT EAT ANYTHING YOU CANNOT POSITIVELY IDENTIFY AND
KNOW TO BE SAFE.
• [6] Familiarise yourself with the plants that are listed on the endangered
species list for your area. Apart from being unethical, it is also illegal to pick
endangered plant species.

Text 3
Foraging in Hong Kong
[1] Wanda Huang is an experienced Hong Kong forager who knows how to
identify edible and medicinal plants. Huang tries to incorporate foraged food
and materials into her daily life and avoids processed and synthetic products as
much as possible. She even makes her own wine and shampoos.
[2] Huang’s interest in foraging started when she was a child in Canada and her
father took her on outings and taught her how to identify herbs and plants in
the wild. “We picked blueberries and made pancakes for breakfast, we made tea
from pine needles and pine cones, and then we cut the pine cones for the nuts. It
was, for me, such a fun experience growing up,” she says fondly. “And we don’t
have to spend time farming — constantly ploughing the land and sowing seeds.
Foraging happens naturally, just like when humans were hunters and
gatherers,” Huang says.
[3] The vegetables we grow today originated from wild plants which had long
roots that penetrated deep into the soil. This means they absorbed a wide range
of nutrients and trace minerals from the soil. Huang says that over time,
commercial farming has produced bigger, sweeter, and faster-growing vegetables
but their roots have shortened. As a result, they no longer absorb all of the trace
minerals and nutrients found deep in the soil. “This is why it’s healthier to eat
wild plants than store-bought vegetables,” Huang says.
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

[4] Huang holds foraging workshops, which are particularly welcomed by chefs
from high-end restaurants. “There’s real interest from the food and beverage
industry in Hong Kong and they’re fascinated about what is edible around
them,” Huang says. Uwe Opocensky, the chef-owner of a restaurant in Sheung
Wan, says, “the taste is much deeper because the plants grow in a natural
environment and the flavour is really related to the soil.”
[5] Hong Kong provides rich pickings for foragers because of its high
biodiversity. The territory lies in the subtropical zone, which means it provides
ideal conditions for both tropical plants and plants that grow in colder climates.
Apart from collecting wild plants for food, people also forage for a wide range
of medicinal plants to use in Chinese medicine or dietary therapy. The local
herbal tea, 24 flavours, is a good example of how rich Hong Kong is in wild
herbs and medicinal plants.
[6] Nevertheless, it is hard for Hong Kong people to incorporate foraging into
their lifestyle because they work such long hours and simply do not have the
time. “People now go to the supermarket and eat bananas from Chile and pak
choi from the Mainland. They’ve lost their connection with the environment.”
Huang says. It is mainly elderly villagers who still possess local knowledge about
edible wild plants. Huang is sad that most people do not see this knowledge as
valuable. “To me, foraging is not about making money but about re-establishing
our connection to the environment and our culture,” Huang says.
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

Questions from the Internet
[1] Naturalist and avid forager John Wright answers questions from the
internet about the fun of finding your own food and the surprising delights
growing outside.
[2] @13happy_mushroom asks: How did you get into foraging?
[3] It was mushrooms that first got me interested. I encountered a mushroom
and was annoyed that I didn’t know what it was. So, I took it home, bought a
book, and managed to identify the species. I’ve carried on ever since. I started
teaching evening classes and now I lead mushroom picking trips and I’m
currently working on my ninth nature guidebook.
[4] @nature_gurl asks: What’s the appeal of finding wild food?
[5] It’s a gentle way for people to go out and engage with the natural world, but
there’s so much more to it. Foraging has a massive sense of freedom and release
from modern day life. A connection to nature is something very special that, in
my eyes, is a privilege and I’m lucky enough to have found a way to make a living
from it.
[6] @eat_to_live1234 asks: What are the benefits of foraging?

[7] Foraging naturally slows you down to become more observant and you gain
an appreciation for the little things which, for me, are the most important. The
physical activity involved in searching for wild edibles in nature provides a
low-impact way to move your body while enjoying the great outdoors. Foraging
also has some mental health benefits. Spending time in green spaces can help
reduce stress, help people cope with anxiety, and provide relief from depression,
as well as improve overall mood and well-being.
[8] @EarthFirst2024 asks: There seems to be a trend in people choosing to
forage. Why do you think this is?
[9] I think food in general has become something people pay more attention to.
A new respect for ourselves with regard to how we treat our bodies, has pushed
people towards smaller producers of better quality food. Small cottage
industries and producers are now more popular with organic and natural
processes being favoured, and there’s nothing more organic than foraged wild
food!

Paragraph 2（第二段）
Personal Background（個人背景）
Huang’s interest in foraging started when she was a child in Canada and her
father took her on outings and taught her how to identify herbs and plants in
the wild.
Huang 對野外採集的興趣始於她在加拿大的童年時期；當時她的父親會帶她
外出，並教她如何辨認野外的香草和植物。
Quotation / Memory（引述／回憶）
“We picked blueberries and made pancakes for breakfast, we made tea from pine
needles and pine cones, and then we cut the pine cones for the nuts.
「我們會採藍莓，然後做班戟當早餐；我們會用松針和松果泡茶，之後又把松
果切開取出堅果。」
Quotation / Reflection（引述／感想）
It was, for me, such a fun experience growing up,” she says fondly.
她深情地說：「對我來說，那是成長過程中非常有趣的經歷。」
Quotation / Contrast（引述／對比）
“And we don’t have to spend time farming — constantly ploughing the land and
sowing seeds.
「而且我們不需要花時間耕種——不用不斷犁地和播種。」
Quotation / Explanation（引述／解釋）
Foraging happens naturally, just like when humans were hunters and
gatherers,” Huang says.
Huang 說：「野外採集是自然發生的，就像人類還是狩獵採集者時一樣。」

Paragraph 3（第三段）
Background（背景）
The vegetables we grow today originated from wild plants which had long roots
that penetrated deep into the soil.
我們今天種植的蔬菜源自野生植物，而那些野生植物擁有能深入土壤的長
根
Explanation（解釋）
This means they absorbed a wide range of nutrients and trace minerals from the
soil.
這意味著它們能從土壤中吸收多種營養和微量礦物質。
Expert View（專家觀點）
Huang says that over time, commercial farming has produced bigger, sweeter,
and faster-growing vegetables but their roots have shortened.
Huang 表示，隨著時間推移，商業農業培育出更大、更甜、生長更快的蔬菜，
但它們的根卻變短了。
Consequence（後果）
As a result, they no longer absorb all of the trace minerals and nutrients found
deep in the soil.
結果，它們不再能吸收土壤深處所有的微量礦物質和營養。
Quotation / Conclusion（引述／結論）
“This is why it’s healthier to eat wild plants than store-bought vegetables,”
Huang says.
Huang 說：「這就是為甚麼吃野生植物比吃商店購買的蔬菜更健康。」

Question 3（問題三）
Question（問題）
@eat_to_live1234 asks: What are the benefits of foraging?
@eat_to_live1234 問：野外採集有甚麼好處？
Answer / Main Point（回答／重點）
Foraging naturally slows you down to become more observant and you gain an
appreciation for the little things which, for me, are the most important.
野外採集自然會讓你放慢腳步，變得更善於觀察；你也會學懂欣賞細微事物
，而對我來說，這些細微事物才是最重要的。
Physical Benefit（身體益處）
The physical activity involved in searching for wild edibles in nature provides a

先看 Text 2 的整體功能
Text 2 的開頭先解釋：
Foraging is identifying, collecting, and eating plants like herbs, fruits, and
nuts that grow wild in nature.
這一句是 definition 定義，
先把 foraging 的基本意思說清楚。
接着下面標題是 Foraging Guidelines，然後列出一系列規則，例如：
● Never start solo.
● Familiarise yourself with the herbs, bushes, and trees around you.
● Learn to identify poisonous plants.
● Familiarise yourself with endangered species.
● Don’t be greedy.
● Know the Law.
整篇 Text 2 的語氣很像 beginner guide，也就是給初學者看的入門指南。
它沒有假設讀者已經懂得分辨植物、懂法律、懂安全規則。

B 說 are new to foraging，即是「剛開始學習 foraging 的人」。
這和原文非常吻合，因為 Text 2 的第一條 guideline 就說：
Never start solo. It’s essential to begin by partnering up with a local expert...
這句裡的 begin 很重要。它直接指向「開始學習的人」。
如果讀者已經是專家，文章就不需要說「開始時要找 local expert」。
另外，文章也提醒讀者：
DO NOT EAT ANYTHING YOU CANNOT POSITIVELY IDENTIFY
AND KNOW TO BE SAFE.
這是非常基礎但非常關鍵的安全提醒。
它假設讀者可能還未懂得準確辨認植物，所以要用最強烈的語氣提醒。
Text 2 還有法律提醒：
it is illegal to cut, pick, or uproot any plant... from within a country park area
without express permission.
這些都屬於初學者需要知道的基本規則。整篇文章的核心讀者就是：想開始
foraging，但需要安全、道德、法律指引的人。

definition + guidelines + law = inform。
